activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Emergency agencies advise unplugging computers and other electronics during a power cut, because a surge of electricity when the power returns can damage them.
story:
The lights at Grandpa's house went out at half past seven, right in the middle of Grayson's turn at chess. The whole room dropped into blue darkness, and the old fridge in the kitchen stopped its humming so suddenly that the silence felt loud.

"Power cut," Grandpa said, calm as anything. He felt along the shelf and found the fat candle and the box of matches. "Happens out here when the wind gets up like this. We'll be fine."

Grayson stared at the dark television, the dark computer in the corner, the little lamp his grandpa used for reading. Then he remembered Ciara, back in October, when a storm had knocked out the power on their street for a whole night. She had gone around her house pulling plugs out of the wall, and when he'd asked her why, she had said, "Emergency agencies say to unplug computers and electronics during a power cut, because when the power comes back on, the surge of electricity can damage them." He hadn't really believed her then. It had sounded like one of those rules adults invent for no reason.

"Grandpa," he said, "can I borrow the candle?"

He carried the flame into the corner, warm wax smell following him, and knelt by the desktop computer. He was hesitant at first, because Grandpa loved that machine and Grayson didn't want to look like he was fiddling with it. But he pulled the plug from the wall anyway. Then the television. Then the kettle, the microwave, the radio on the windowsill.

"What are you doing back there?" Grandpa called.

"Unplugging things. Ciara told me the power coming back can send a surge through them and wreck the electronics. So you're supposed to unplug them during the cut."

"Huh," said Grandpa, and Grayson heard him settle back into his chair. "Well, that's one for the city kids to teach us."

They played chess by candlelight after that, hunched over the board, coat buttons cold under Grayson's fingers. Grandpa told a long story about a blackout from decades ago, and about how he had once, at Grayson's age, blamed a friend named Nathaniel for something Grayson himself had broken. "I never did fix that right," Grandpa said, moving his bishop. "Couldn't articulate it at the time. Still can't, really." Grayson wasn't sure what to say, so he just took the bishop.

Around nine, the lights blazed back on. The fridge roared awake, the lamp switched itself on, and everything in the wall sockets jumped at once. Then, from the back room, there was a crack, a pop like a firecracker, and a thin thread of smoke rose from Grandpa's old radio, the one still plugged in by the sofa, the one Grayson hadn't noticed in the dark.

They stood over it together. Grayson's heart was hammering, but underneath the fright was something else: Ciara had been right, and if he hadn't gone around pulling plugs, that crack would have come from the computer too.

"Well," Grandpa said. He put a hand on Grayson's shoulder. "Go get the broom, and then call your friend Ciara and tell her she saved my chess computer."

Grayson was already reaching for the phone.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: Prithee is a squeezed-together form of "I pray thee" and means please.
story:
Alexis sat at the kitchen table with a photocopy of A Midsummer Night's Dream spread in front of him and a pencil that had already gone blunt. Mr. Sánchez had assigned each student one scene to paraphrase into modern English, and Alexis had gotten the part where Helena begs Demetrius to treat her like a dog. His little sister's bug jar sat at the corner of the table, where a fat larva chewed a milkweed leaf, but even that was less confusing than "I am your spaniel; and, Demetrius, / The more you beat me, I will fawn on you." He read it aloud three times and still could not figure out how to say it like a normal person.

"Take a break," his mother said, sliding a plate of toast toward him. "You've been frowning at that paper for an hour." He shook his head. Mr. Sánchez had promised the paraphrases would be performed out loud on Friday, and if Alexis stood up and read nonsense, everyone would hear it. He wanted to get it right, not almost right.

He texted Marielle, who had the same scene. Do you get the "prithee" part? She wrote back a minute later: I keep reading it like the character is weird. Maybe she's cursed? Alexis stared at the word. Prithee. He flipped through his stack of photocopies and found other speeches, hunting for the pattern. Where characters said "I pray thee," they were asking for something. Where they said "prithee," they were also asking for something, in exactly the same spots. He tested it against Helena's lines, swapping one word for the other, and the whole sentence still worked. It was like discovering the two words were squeezed together versions of each other. He typed back: I don't think she's cursed. Prithee means please. She's just being polite, and he's being horrible to her anyway. Marielle sent back a row of exclamation marks and one word: finally.

The doorbell rang. Elly stood on the step holding a folded note, since her phone had been taken away for a week. The note said she had the rude mechanicals' scene and was stuck too, and could she please work at his table, and she promised not to touch the bug jar. She sat down, arranged her paper so its edges were perfectly symmetrical with the table's edge, and got to work.

When Marielle called later, Alexis could hear her reading her paraphrase in a shaking voice: "Please, just let me come with you. I'll follow you even if you're mean to me." Elly nudged him and whispered, "Tell her that's good." He passed it on, and Marielle's voice steadied. Down at the end of the table, the larva had stopped chewing and hung motionless from the leaf. "It's turning into a butterfly," Elly said. "Tonight, maybe." Alexis picked his pencil back up. "Then we'd better finish before it does."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
story:
The party spilled across two backyards, Brody's family and Zane's, because their parents had been neighbors long enough to knock down the fence between them. Brody carried a bowl of fruit toward the long table and paused at the stone wall at the far edge of the yard, where pale green lichen had crept over the rocks in rough circles. He wondered how long it had taken to grow, whether it was older than he was. A voice behind him said, "You'll miss the giving of the gifts," and Zane pulled him back toward the crowd.

In Zane's family, gifts weren't ripped open in front of everyone. They were handed over with both hands, received with both hands, and set aside to be opened later, which drove Brody a little crazy. His aunt had already pressed a wrapped box into his palms that way, and he had been watching all afternoon to see if everyone did it, and so far, every single person did. At dinner there was another puzzle: Zane's grandmother served the youngest guests first, and nobody started eating until she lifted her own fork. Brody filed both rules away, the way he collected facts about lichen and weather.

Then he saw the problem. His little cousin, four years old and sticky with cake, was standing beside Zane's uncle, and one of the visiting grown-ups reached out cheerfully to ruffle the boy's hair. Zane moved faster than Brody had ever seen him move in gym class, stepping between them with a plate of mango.

"Sorry," Zane said, "in Thailand the head is sacred, so touching someone's head, even patting a kid, can be rude. My uncle's from Bangkok."

The grown-up pulled his hand back and apologized, and the uncle smiled and waved it off, but Brody noticed he had gone very still for a moment before that. So it mattered, even here, even at a backyard party two yards from the lichen wall. Brody tested it in his head: he had patted his cousin's head a dozen times today, and nobody had said a word to him. Maybe because his cousin wasn't Thai? Or because family was different from guests? He couldn't see the rule itself, only its shadow, and he wanted to know where the edges were.

After dinner he found Zane by the stone wall, supervising a game where the little kids tried to balance pebbles on their palms. "Both hands for gifts," Brody said, counting on his fingers, "grandmother eats first, and no touching heads. Anything else I'm going to get wrong at your birthday?"

Zane laughed and handed him a pebble, flat and gray and perfectly transparent where the sun caught its edge. "Balance this," he said. "I'll tell you when you fail."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
Eleanor slid the green binder across the library table until it bumped Joshua's elbow. "Mr. Nguyen says we have to use a primary source," she whispered. "That means something written by a person who was actually there."

Joshua flipped through the photocopies inside. Most of them were dull, a list of supplies, a frugal housewife's account of every penny spent on flour. Then he stopped at one page. "Listen to this. It's from a settler's diary, March 1848. 'Word has reached us of gold in California. My brother talks of nothing else.'"

"California," Eleanor repeated. She pulled the timeline sheet from her folder and smoothed it flat. The paper had a long arrow pointing west with the word MIGRATION printed above it, and a fat cluster of dots near the far edge. "So people moved for farmland. That's what our textbook chapter says."

"Not this guy's brother." Joshua tapped the diary line. "He came for money. Gold fever, that's what the diary calls it."

Eleanor frowned at the timeline. The dots were thickest at the very end of the arrow, but the chapter title said nothing about gold. Maybe the book was just... incomplete? She needed to know what actually pulled all those people west, and one diary line wasn't proof. She raised her hand, and Mr. Nguyen came over.

"I have a question about evidence," Eleanor said. "If one diary says the brother wanted gold, is that enough to explain the big arrow?"

"One source illustrates one family's reasons," Mr. Nguyen said. "What would you need to confirm it?"

Eleanor thought. "More sources? From different people?" She marched to the computer catalog and typed GOLD CALIFORNIA. A memoir by a woman who crossed the plains in 1849 appeared, and she carried the heavy book back to the table. Vada, at the next table, leaned over to see.

"She's finding out why people went west," Vada told Joshua. "Ask her about the diary."

Eleanor flipped the memoir's pages carefully. In the second chapter, the woman wrote that her husband sold their shop after hearing that gold had been discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848. Eleanor read the date twice. Her finger moved to the timeline. The thick cluster of dots sat right after 1848, on the western end.

"It fits," she said. "One diary, one memoir, the dates match up. Gold was found in January 1848, and then all those dots show up." She drew a light pencil line connecting 1848 to the cluster, then checked it against the diary's March entry.

"So the textbook just skipped it?" Joshua asked.

Eleanor grinned. "The textbook gave one reason. The primary sources gave the other one." She started writing her paragraph, then paused and slid the memoir across to Vada, who had been craning her neck. "You can share. There's a good part on page forty about the wagon."

Vada turned to page forty and gasped. "She brought her cat the whole way?"

"Every single mile," Eleanor said, and went back to her pencil.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fast growth during puberty often causes stretch marks, thin lines on the skin that are common and usually fade over time.
story:
Taylor discovered the lines on a Tuesday morning, standing in front of the bathroom mirror in her pajamas. They ran sideways across her hips, thin and pale, like the marks a pencil eraser leaves behind on a page. She pulled her shirt down and up three times to check whether they disappeared when she wasn't looking. They didn't.

At school, in Ms. Shin's health classroom, the posters showed diagrams of hearts and food groups, and the word PUBERTY was written on the board in blue marker. Taylor sat between Sarina and Caiden, keeping her hoodie zipped to her chin even though the room was warm and smelled like disinfectant and orange peel from somebody's snack. Ms. Shin was explaining that some changes were voluntary, like choosing to lift your hand or speak up, while others happened on their own, without any decision at all. Taylor thought about her hips. Nobody had asked her permission for those lines.

She passed a folded note to Sarina under the desk. Do you ever get marks on your skin that you didn't put there? Sarina read it, then wrote back slowly, her pencil pressing so hard it tore a little: My sister had them on her legs when she grew like four inches in one summer. She said everybody gets them and they fade. Taylor read the note twice, then a third time, and felt something in her chest loosen, though not all the way. Sarina's sister was seventeen. Seventeen seemed very far away, like an answer written on the last page of a textbook.

After class, Taylor stayed behind while Caiden swept the spilled glitter off the group table, a punishment for flicking it at Sarina during the video. "Ms. Shin," Taylor said, staring at the diagram of the heart because looking at the actual poster was easier than looking at the actual teacher, "are stretch marks normal?" Ms. Shin smiled and said, "Stretch marks? Very common during growth spurts." That was all, and somehow that was enough.

On the bus home, Taylor did the math the way she did equations in her head, lining up the facts like numbers. She had grown two shoe sizes since June. Her jeans that fit in September now stopped at her ankles. Fast growth, lines on skin. It wasn't a mystery with a hidden villain; it was just her body doing what bodies did, faster than her skin seemed to expect. Still, she remembered a girl in fifth grade, the one everyone had whispered about, and Taylor felt a small hot knot of shame when she recalled laughing along. She hadn't known anything then. She knew something now, and knowing made the memory sit differently, the way a word you finally learn makes you hear it everywhere.

That evening her mom knocked on her door and sat on the edge of the bed, holding a folded towel. "You okay? You've been quiet since dinner." Taylor pulled up the hem of her shirt a few inches, just far enough. Her mom looked, nodded, and said, "I had those too, right there. They fade, you know. Mine mostly did." Taylor studied her mother's hips where her sweater hung, and the lines there were so faint she had to squint, like footprints after snow has almost melted.

Later, in her notebook, under the equation homework she'd finished, Taylor wrote a message she might or might not give to the fifth-grade girl if she ever saw her again: I'm sorry I laughed. I have them too now, and they're nothing. She read it over, folded it in quarters, and tucked it into the drawer with her pencils, deciding later whether it would ever be sent. Then she changed into her softest pajamas, unzipped her hoodie for good, and stood in front of the mirror with the bathroom light on, tracing one thin line with her finger until her mom called, "Lights out in ten, sleepyhead, or you'll turn into a bear and hibernate till spring."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
story:
Camille stood in the living room of the blue house on Marigold Lane and realized she could not remember its number. Ms. Farah-Ali was pulling on her coat, and her husband was hunting for his keys, and little Blaze was already negotiating hard.

"One more show," Blaze announced from the couch. "Dinosaur Hotel. It's my favorite. It's basically my whole life."

"Bedtime is eight," said Ms. Farah-Ali. "Camille, snacks are in the cupboard, and my number is on the fridge."

"Wait," Camille said. "What's your address here? The whole thing, with the number."

Ms. Farah-Ali paused with one arm in a sleeve. "Fourteen Marigold Lane. Why, sweetheart?"

Camille pulled the notepad off the phone table and wrote it down, adjusting the paper so it sat flat beneath the phone. "My mom said if you ever have to call nine-one-one, the first thing the dispatcher asks for is the address of the emergency. So you have to know it before anything happens." It seemed like a strange thing to worry about in a living room with warm lamps and a sleeping cat, but writing it down made her feel steadier, like the difference between guessing and knowing.

"It sounds arbitrary, which number a house gets," Ms. Farah-Ali said, smiling, "but I suppose it isn't, not when it matters. All right. Fourteen Marigold Lane. We're two streets away, back by ten."

The door closed, and Blaze immediately began a campaign. He explained that eight o'clock was a made-up concept, that dinosaur documentaries were educational, and that big kids got to stay up. Camille let him finish, because interrupting seemed rude, and then she said, "One episode. Then teeth, then bed." Blaze pumped his fist like he had won a championship.

He was quiet for exactly nine minutes. Then, during a scene about a triceratops, he decided to bounce on the couch cushions "like a hadrosaur," lost his footing, and cracked his chin hard on the armrest. The sound was awful. Blaze howled, and blood began running from a split in his lip, bright red and a lot of it, more blood than Camille had ever seen outside of a movie.

She grabbed a dish towel and pressed it gently under his lip, the way her mom did for nosebleeds, and told him to lean forward. He kept crying. The bleeding didn't slow. Her hands were shaking, and part of her brain insisted it was just a split lip, kids got split lips all the time, but another part kept counting how much red there was on the towel. She picked up the phone and dialed nine-one-one.

"Nine-one-one, what's the address of your emergency?"

The question came first, exactly as her mother had said it would. Camille's eyes went straight to the notepad. "Fourteen Marigold Lane," she read. "I'm babysitting. He's four. He hit his chin on the couch and his lip is bleeding a lot and it won't stop."

The dispatcher's voice was calm and quick. She asked Camille to keep the towel pressed and firm, told her an ambulance was on its way, and stayed on the line. Camille sat on the floor with Blaze's head against her shoulder, holding the towel, counting his breaths out loud because it gave them both something to do. "Fifty-two, fifty-three," she said, and Blaze, sniffling, whispered, "This is the worst episode of Dinosaur Hotel ever."

The paramedics arrived in eight minutes, which Camille knew because she watched the clock the whole time. They took one look, cleaned the cut, and said it was small but stubborn, exactly the kind that bleeds dramatically and then gives up. Blaze got a shiny wrap of gauze that he immediately declared his "battle bandage." When Ms. Farah-Ali hurried in, pale and breathless, Blaze lifted his chin and said, "I survived. Did Camille tell you I survived?"

Camille handed over the bloody towel and the notepad with the address still sitting under the phone. "I wrote it down before you left," she said, "just in case."

Ms. Farah-Ali looked at the notepad for a long moment, then at Camille. "Next Friday," she said. "Same rate, plus extra. Blaze, bedtime."

"Dinosaur Hotel," Blaze countered from the couch, gauze gleaming. "Season finale."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
story:
The folding chairs were still set up on the grass when the last cars pulled away, and Peyton stayed behind while her dad talked with the funeral director near the gate. She had the newspaper clipping in her coat pocket, the one her aunt had cut out. She'd read it six times since Tuesday, and one line still stopped her cold every time: before she married, her grandmother had spent four years working as a sailor on cargo ships. Four years. Peyton had eaten Sunday dinner with this woman maybe three hundred times, and Grandma had never once said a word about the ocean.

"Is that the obituary?" Danica asked, sitting down in the chair beside her. Kloe squeezed in on the other side, careful not to knock the flowers. Peyton held it out so they could see. "It's a notice that runs in the paper when someone dies," she said. "It tells about their life. Family, work, the stuff they loved." Kloe squinted at the page. "It says she was a sailor. Your grandma was a sailor and you didn't know?"

"That's the part that's bugging me," Peyton said. Her brain felt lethargic from crying and from the casseroles, but something was ticking over anyway. "People don't just forget four years on ships. So either she deliberately never talked about it, or she did talk about it and I missed it." She devised a test right there, out loud, because that was how she did her best thinking. "If it was a secret, there'd be nothing at the house. If it wasn't, there'd be traces. My criterion is simple: one single object that only makes sense if she was a sailor."

Mr. Aquino, the neighbor who'd driven Grandma to bingo every Friday, came over with a thermos of hot chocolate and three cups, because he'd noticed the girls rubbing their hands. "You look like you're plotting something," he said. Peyton showed him the clipping. He laughed, a big rolling laugh that seemed too loud for a cemetery until he got it under control. "She never told you about the time the ship nearly sank in a storm, either, I bet. She told me that story four times. She'd say, 'If the world thinks you're just somebody's grandmother, let it think that.'"

On Monday Peyton searched the house with Danica and Kloe as backup. In the cedar chest, under the quilts, they found a brass pocket compass, a photograph of Grandma at twenty-three in a rain slicker grinning on a ship's deck, and a folded paper boat, brittle with age, tucked inside a paperback novel. Peyton held the boat up. "Criterion met," she said, and Danica cheered so loudly the dog barked.

The following Sunday they went back to the cemetery with the paper boat, and Peyton set it on the headstone where the wind couldn't take it, weighted with a pebble. "Fair winds, Grandma," she said. Kloe leaned in and whispered, "Do you think she'd rather have had the hot chocolate?"

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
story:
Stella stood at her grandmother's counter with a whole onion in front of her and a plan in her head. Grandma was out in the garden picking basil, so tonight's pasta sauce was Stella's job, start to finish. Her cousin Remi sat on a stool nearby, watching like the whole thing was a show. "Curved fingers," Stella said to herself, bending her fingertips under so her knuckles stuck out like little claws. "The knife rides along the knuckles, and the onion can't get me." She set the blade against the vegetable and let it glide down, and a neat slice fell open on the board.

The onion fought back anyway. Its stinging spray rose up and thwarted her plan to keep crying out of the recipe, so she tried an idea. She put the cutting board near the open window, where a breeze came through, and chopped facing away from herself. The stinging faded. "Ha," she said, wiping one eye. "The wind carries it off." Remi leaned over the slices and said, "You look like you lost a fight." "The onion's the antagonist here," Stella said. "And I'm winning."

She softened the onion in olive oil, crushed the tomatoes in with her hands, and added salt and a leaf of Grandma's basil. Then she clapped a lid on the pot, turned the heat low, and went to set the table, because her parents were arriving at six and the sauce needed to be ready by then. Remi timed it on the kitchen clock. The pot sat there quietly, rattling its lid.

At half past five she lifted the lid and stirred. The sauce was thin, pale orange, and sloshed around like soup. Remi dipped a spoon in and made a face. "It's supposed to be thicker than this. Grandma's coats the spoon." Stella stared at the pot, thinking. The lid had been on the whole time. Steam had been knocking at it, fogging the glass, going nowhere. She remembered the window and the onion sting, how the wind had carried that away, and something clicked. With the lid off, the steam could rise out and away, and whatever stayed behind would have to be thicker. It was worth testing. She took the lid clean off and turned the burner up a notch.

"Twenty-eight minutes," Remi announced, watching the clock. The kitchen filled with a warm tomato smell, and little wisps curled up from the surface and vanished. Stella stirred every few minutes and watched the level sink, slow but real. When she dragged the spoon through, the sauce left a clean trail that closed lazily instead of flooding back.

At two minutes to six, the front door opened and her parents came in with the pasta. Grandma appeared behind them, still holding a bunch of basil, and looked over Stella's shoulder at the pot. Stella lifted the spoon and let the sauce fall in one heavy red ribbon. "Lid off the whole time," she said. Grandma smiled and reached for the plates.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses, which is one reason washing with soap removes them better than rinsing with water alone.
story:
Georgia had been home from school for three days, and the kitchen had become her whole world. She sat at the table with a mug of warm honey water, watching her little brother dunk his hands under the running tap for about four seconds before reaching for the cookie jar. She cleared her throat, and he froze.

"Washing," he said, holding up dripping hands.

"That's rinsing," Georgia said. "There's a difference." She got up slowly, because her legs still felt like wet sand, and took two saucers from the cupboard. On one she smeared a blob of butter. On the other, another blob, the same size. "Watch." She ran the first saucer under the tap and rubbed it with her finger. The butter stayed, smeared around in a greasy film. Then she took the dish soap, put one drop on the second saucer, and worked it with her fingers under the water. The butter broke apart and slid off, and the saucer came out squeaky clean. "That's what soap does to the flu virus," she said. "It breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds it. That's why washing with soap works better than water alone."

Her brother squinted at the saucers. "So the virus is like butter?"

"Kind of. It mimics it, at least for this." She pointed at the second saucer. "Water alone can't get rid of the fatty layer. Soap can."

There was a silence that Georgia found interesting. Her brother looked at his shoes, then at the cookie jar, then at his shoes again. Out the window, Mr. Ong was yanking at the invasive vine that had crawled over his fence all summer, and the radio on the counter murmured something about agriculture and this year's harvest, but her brother's ears had gone pink.

"I've been doing the tap thing," he admitted. "At school. After Kaiya and Sky got sick and everyone said wash your hands." He held up his hands again, as if they might testify against him.

Georgia sat back down and pushed the cookie jar toward him. "Take one. Then soap, twenty seconds, both hands. Deal?"

He took two cookies, because he was eight and that was math he understood, and marched to the sink. She heard the pump of the soap dispenser, the splashing, even a little humming that was probably him counting. He came back and held his hands out for inspection, smelling of lemon suds.

"Clean," Georgia said, and handed him the dry saucers to stack.

"Georgia," he said, very seriously, "the butter one was gross."

"The butter one was science," she said, and drank the last of her honey water.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
Kate despised the waiting room more than the exam room, because in the waiting room nothing happened except the clock and her stomach. She had been here three times in six weeks for the same thing: headaches, a sour stomach, sleeping badly. The tests always came back normal, which was starting to feel like an insult. She sat flipping a ragged magazine while her mom filled out forms, and she watched Dr. Iyer's office door, waiting.

This time, Dr. Iyer pulled up her chart instead of ordering more blood work. "Kate, I want to ask you about the weeks before these headaches started. Anything change? School, home, anything."

Kate hesitated. "There's a group chat," she finally said. "Some kids from class. It goes all night. If I leave it, I miss things. If I stay, I'm up until one in the morning reading messages, some of them about me." She hadn't meant to say that last part out loud.

Dr. Iyer nodded slowly. "That sounds like real stress, not the temporary kind that passes after a test. Here's something worth knowing. When you're under stress, your adrenal glands make more of a hormone called cortisol. That's normal. But when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high, and that can leave you feeling run down." She tapped the screen. "Your body's been running an alarm for six weeks. That could be what your stomach's been telling us."

Kate's reasoning started turning before they even left the office. If the group chat was keeping her cortisol high, then the headaches weren't random; they had a cause she could actually test. In the car she asked her mom for a notebook, and that night she drew two columns: nights she stayed in the chat past midnight, and mornings she woke up with a headache. She also wrote one word at the top of the page, from something Dr. Iyer had mentioned on the way out: boundaries. Kate wasn't sure yet what her version of that looked like, but she wanted to find out.

By Thursday she had four rows of data and a pattern she could see with her own eyes: every late night lined up with a headache morning, and the two nights she'd logged off at nine, nothing. On Friday she told Arthur and Madden at lunch, phone face-down on the table between them. "I'm doing an experiment," she said. "Nine o'clock, chat off, every night this weekend. If my headaches stop, that's my coping plan, and you two are my witnesses." Madden slid his own phone across the table and turned it off with a click. "Witnessed," he said.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
story:
The waiting room smelled like bandages and orange cleaner, and Benjamin sat with his right arm resting on his knee, six weeks of signatures and doodles marching down the fiberglass cast. Camryn had drawn a dragon near the wrist on day two. Baylee had written GET WELL OR ELSE in green marker, which had made him laugh so hard his mom had shushed him from across the room. Now the whole thing was coming off, and he should have been excited, except for the saw.

He had heard it through the wall twice already that morning. It shrieked like a circular saw cutting plywood, long angry bursts that made his spine prickle. A little kid in the corner had started crying after the second burst, and the kid's mother was rubbing his back in slow circles.

"Benjamin?" A nurse held the door open, clipboard against her hip.

He stood up and followed her down the hall, and when she set a metal tray on the counter he saw the saw itself, squat and plug-in, with a round blade behind a guard. "That's the same kind of saw my dad uses in the garage," he said. "For plywood."

"I promise it's not the same kind at all." She plugged it in, and the little kid's mother appeared in the doorway with the crying boy, who apparently had a cast coming off too.

"Could he watch yours first?" the mother asked the nurse. "He's scared, and I thought maybe seeing it happen to someone brave would help."

Benjamin looked at the kid, maybe six years old, tears streaked sideways down his cheeks. "Sure," he said. "But, um. Can you tell us why that won't cut my arm? Because I'd honestly like to know too."

The nurse smiled and lifted the saw so they could both see the blade. "The blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning," she said. "That's how it cuts through hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath."

Back and forth instead of spinning. Benjamin turned that over while the nurse positioned his arm on the padded table. A spinning blade would grab skin and pull itself through it, he reasoned, the way his dad's saw chewed into wood. A blade that only wiggled could batter rigid fiberglass until it cracked apart, but skin was soft and loose; it would just shake with it. That had to be the trick. He couldn't see the vibration itself, but he could test the idea.

"Wait," he said. "Before you start. Can I touch the blade while it's running? Just my fingertip?"

"Hold it flat against the blade, light pressure," the nurse said, and she powered it on. The noise was exactly as awful as it had sounded through the wall, a furious buzzing, but Benjamin pressed his finger against the moving blade and felt nothing but a strange tickle, like a phone vibrating in his pocket. He laughed out loud from relief.

The little boy crept closer, wiping his nose. "It didn't cut you?"

"Not even a little. Wanna feel?" Benjamin held out his hand, and the boy touched one cautious finger to the buzzing blade, then broke into a gap-toothed grin.

"All right, brave guys," the nurse said. "Who's first?"

"Me," said Benjamin, laying his arm flat and giving the kid a thumbs-up with his free hand. "Watch close."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
story:
Cooper curled his fingers into a claw and set the blade against the onion, the way Ms. MacLeod had shown them. "Knuckles forward, fingertips tucked," she said as she moved between the stations, and Cooper noticed that when his knuckles led, the knife had nowhere dangerous to go. The onion resisted at first, then gave way in thin half-moons that filled the cutting board. Beside him, Clementine was mincing garlic into tiny pieces, and Skye had the pan heating on the stove already.

Their group had drawn tomato sauce from scratch, and Cooper wanted theirs to be the batch the whole class tasted at the end. He dumped the onion and the garlic into the hot pan together, and everything sizzled loudly. He stirred and stirred, proud of how fast it was cooking.

The smell turned on him. Something sharp and acrid rose off the pan, nothing like the sweet smell from the recipe photo. When Skye tasted the finished sauce, she grimaced. "It's bitter," she said. "Like, actually bitter, not just tomato-y."

Cooper stared at the pan and turned the afternoon over in his head. Clementine's group had started at the same time, with the same ingredients, but their sauce smelled good from across the room. He walked past their station on the way to the sink and glanced over. Their onions were in the pan alone, soft and golden, and the garlic was still sitting on the cutting board, waiting. That was the difference. Their first attempt had gone in together on high heat, and his had too, but the garlic had not survived it the same way the onion did. "The garlic burns way faster than the onion," he said when he got back, "and it tastes bitter when it's burnt. We cooked them the same, but they're not the same." It sounded almost too simple to be true, but the evidence was on the other counter, smelling delicious.

"That's plausible," Skye admitted, scraping the bitter sauce into the waste bowl. "So we put the garlic in after the onions soften."

Ms. MacLeod passed by and nodded at their second onion, already coming apart under Cooper's claw grip. "There's sauce in the pantry if this batch goes wrong," she offered, but Cooper shook his head.

They started over. Onions in first, alone, heat turned down, Cooper stirring while Clementine chopped fresh garlic and Skye opened a new can of tomatoes. The onions went soft and translucent, and only then did Cooper sweep the garlic in, counting slowly to himself while the kitchen filled with a smell that made his stomach growl.

When it was their turn at the tasting table, Cooper watched the teacher take her spoonful. Ms. MacLeod paused, then went back for a second spoonful, and Clementine grabbed Cooper's arm.

"Second spoonful," she whispered. "That's the good sign."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Researchers usually define bullying as hurtful behavior that is repeated and involves an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals.
story:
At Marcus's birthday party, the table was crowded with paper plates and a pitcher of something yellow that smelled like peach nectar. Henry was reaching for a cup when he heard Edison laugh across the room. "Nice shirt, Lena. Did you dress in the dark again?" It was the third time this week someone had said something like that to her, and Lena had stopped answering, which was new.

Henry tried to think it through. If Edison had said it once, it might just be a joke gone wrong; he and Lena had argued before, and arguments between friends blew over. But this kept happening, and Edison was the loudest kid in the grade, while Lena sat alone at lunch now. It wasn't the same thing at all. He thought about the poster outside Ms. Wong's classroom, the one he'd read while waiting for the buses. He hadn't really believed he'd need it.

He carried his cup over to where Lena was standing by the window, pretending to watch the balloons. "Do you want to see if they have more cake in the kitchen?" he asked. She glanced at Edison, then nodded. In the kitchen, Henry kept it short. "What Edison does, calling it joking, I don't think it is. It keeps happening, and it's not like you two are evenly matched. It's bullying." Lena looked at the counter for a while. "I thought maybe I was being too sensitive," she said.

Henry had a plan, or at least the approximate shape of one. Charging at Edison would just start a yelling match, and Ms. Wong wasn't here. Instead, when they went back out, he sat down next to Lena and stayed there. Edison circled by with a remark about her drawing, and Henry said, "Her drawing's better than mine. You've seen it." Then he asked Lena which marker she used for the sky in that picture of the lighthouse, and she started explaining, and Edison drifted off toward the music.

It worked twice more. Whenever Edison came near, Henry didn't shout or lecture; he just moved closer and asked Lena something real, about the comic she was making or the spelling test. Edison got bored of an audience that wasn't reacting. By the time the cake came out, he was arguing with another boy about soccer, and Lena was showing Henry her sketchbook, flipping pages fast, her thumb leaving a small smudge of graphite on each corner.

On Monday, Henry planned to revise his approach based on what he'd learned: you couldn't fix everything in one afternoon, but you could change who a person sat next to. He found Lena at the empty end of the lunch table and set his tray down across from her. She slid her sketchbook over. "So which one do you like better," she asked, "the dragon or the whale?"

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
story:
The booth by the window was the only quiet spot in the whole restaurant, and Luca spread his Spanish notes across the table anyway. Tomorrow first period, Mr. Kaminski's quiz: describe your family and pets in full sentences. He had one night and half a basket of breadsticks. Across from him, Aimee kept glancing at the dessert case like it owed her money.

"You already know all this," she said, tapping his notebook. "You've been muttering about your dog since the garlic bread came."

"Mi perro es blanco y negro," Luca said. "Mi hermana es baja. Mi hermano está cansado." He wrote that last one down, proud of it, because his brother really had collapsed onto the couch the second they got home from the restaurant's parking lot.

The man at the next table set down his coffee and laughed. He was the tenant who lived in the apartment above the restaurant; everyone called him Mr. Kaminski even though he wasn't the teacher, which Luca found confusing in a way he'd stopped asking about. "Did you just tell me your brother is permanently exhausted?" the man said.

Luca stared at his notebook. Permanently? He looked at the sentence. He looked at the other sentences. Mi hermana es baja. Mi hermano está cansado. There was a pattern hiding in there, something he couldn't see directly, and he could feel it circling like a fish under ice. Es showed up with blanco, with baja, with things that stayed true. Estar had appeared exactly once, in the sentence about being tired. Tired was a tonight kind of thing. Tall was a forever kind of thing. He flipped his pencil around and erased, then wrote a test sentence: Mi hermano es alto. Then, underneath: Mi hermano está cansado. He slid the notebook toward Mr. Kaminski and held his breath while the man read it, the way you hold your breath waiting for a bridge to hold.

"Es alto means he is tall," Mr. Kaminski said slowly, nodding. "Está cansado means he is tired. Ser for lasting traits, estar for temporary states." He tapped the page. "Your brother sleeps a lot, but not forever."

Luca copied the two sentences into his notes in big letters and boxed them. Aimee leaned over his shoulder to look, then turned back to the dessert case, where the last slice of chocolate cake was sitting under the glass with a little card that said the case closed at nine. It was 8:52.

"Waiter," she called, raising her hand. "The chocolate one. Please, before it's too late."

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: On geometry diagrams, matching tick marks show sides that are equal in length, and matching arcs show angles that are equal.
story:
Sofia had copied the whole triangle off the board: two sides, a slanted third side, the angle marked between them. Ms. Zhao had drawn hers with a smudgy marker, and half the class was squinting. Sofia wrote "Given: triangle ABC" at the top of her proof and then stopped. Which sides was she supposed to say were equal? She looked back at the board. Ms. Zhao's diagram had little dashes on two of the sides and little curved marks on two angles, and Sofia's notebook had, well, a plain triangle. A very plain, useless triangle.

"You're staring at that thing like it's venomous," said Candice, leaning over from the next desk. "It's paper. It can't bite you."

"It might as well. I can't do the side-angle-side proof if I don't know which sides match. It's like the clues just evaporated on my walk from the board to my seat."

Moshe leaned in from the other side, holding up his own notebook. His diagram was even messier than the board version, but it had the little marks. "These are the clues," he said. "Matching tick marks show sides that are equal in length, and matching arcs show angles that are equal. Mine show two ticks on AB and BC, so those are the equal sides, and the arcs are on angle B and the angle at the other triangle."

Sofia looked from his page to hers. The marks weren't decoration. They were the whole "given." She had copied the shape but left behind the information, which was like copying a recipe but skipping the ingredients list. "Okay, okay. New plan. I prioritize getting the marks down before I write another word of the proof." She went up to the board, which earned her a look from Ms. Zhao that could have curdled milk, but she got a good view, hurried back, and added two ticks to AB and BC and arcs to angle B and its partner.

Then everything lined up. Two sides equal, the angle between them equal, so by side-angle-side the triangles were congruent. She wrote the statements and the reasons in two neat columns, and it actually felt like arguing a case, except the case was about triangles and nobody could object because she had the rules on her side.

Outside the window, a patch of gray lichen crept across the brick ledge, slow and patient, like it had all year to cover its little section of wall. Sofia decided she was going to be faster than the lichen. She raised her hand anyway, just to check one thing about the arcs, and Ms. Zhao came over.

"Show me what you have," said Ms. Zhao.

Sofia slid the notebook across the desk, ticks and all.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In Richard Connell's 1924 story The Most Dangerous Game, the island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and sailors' fear of it hint at the danger waiting there.
story:
Sawyer slid the photocopy across the library table and squinted at the first page like it had personally insulted him. "Mr. Ferreira says we have to find foreshadowing in this story and explain what it suggests. What even counts? Is the weather foreshadowing? Can a sandwich be foreshadowing?"

"Everything is a sandwich if you believe," said Moses, without looking up from his book.

Filip leaned over Sawyer's shoulder. "It's that island story. The hunting one. My brother read it last year and refused to go on our ferry trip afterward."

They were tucked into the back corner of the school library, where the old encyclopedias lived and nobody bothered you unless a teacher was on patrol. Mr. Ferreira had given them one class period to find three clues the author dropped before anything bad happened, and Sawyer had a chronic habit of noticing nothing on the first read. He skimmed the opening again, slower this time, dragging his pencil along the lines.

"Wait," he said. "The yacht captain says the sailors have a weird dread of the place. And look, it has a name." He tapped the page. "Ship-Trap Island. That is not a name a real estate agent would pick."

Filip frowned. "So the author just told us the island is bad? That seems rude. Like a spoiler on purpose."

"That's the point, maybe?" Sawyer sat up straighter, which for Sawyer was practically standing. "The name itself traps ships, or hints it does, and the sailors' fear of the island tells us danger is waiting there before the guy even lands. It's like the author left the porch light on so we'd know somebody's home."

"Terrible porch," Moses said. "Ten out of ten would not visit."

Sawyer flipped forward, testing his idea. He looked for more signals, and there they were: gunshots in the dark water, a conversation about hunting being the best thing in life, a guy named Rainsford who said the world was made of hunters and hounds. Each one seemed to propel the story toward something before it arrived. He wrote ship name = warning on his paper, then crossed out ship name and wrote place name, because the island was the place, and being precise mattered when you were accusing an author of leaving clues.

"Okay, but what does it suggest," Filip said, reading the assignment over his arm. "That's the part I'd bomb. Saying a clue exists isn't the same as saying what it means."

"So we write that the fear of the island suggests the place is dangerous, and the author wanted us uneasy early." Sawyer chewed his pencil. "Is that symbolism too, or just foreshadowing? Could the island symbolize a trap? Moses, is a trap a symbol if it's also literally the plot?"

Moses finally looked up. "You're asking the wrong guy. I'm still on my sandwich theory."

Mr. Ferreira drifted past their table on his patrol, glanced at Sawyer's notes, and raised one eyebrow. "Careful, Mr. Sawyer. You keep noticing things like that, people will start calling you a reader."

"Is that a threat, sir?"

"It's foreshadowing," said Mr. Ferreira, and kept walking.

Sawyer grinned, wrote "the island is a warning sign" at the top of the page, and underlined it twice.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
The family group chat lit up at 4:58, two hours before the dance. Grandma: "Pictures! Lots of pictures!" Dad sent a thumbs up. Zoey's little brother sent a potato emoji, which meant nothing, or possibly meant he'd stolen her charger again. She ignored them all and focused on her getting-ready ritual: hair brushed exactly fifty strokes, the good sweater, the lucky socks. Her stomach had been volatile all afternoon, flipping every time she thought about the gym, the lights, the possibility that Elisha might be there.

In the car, her brother went quiet, which was strange for him. He gripped the seatbelt and said his stomach felt weird and his heart was going fast, and they weren't even at the school yet. "Butterflies," Zoey said, mostly to tease him. He scowled at the window. She pressed two fingers to her own wrist and counted. Fast. Faster than after gym class, and she'd been sitting still for ten minutes. Something invisible was happening to both of them before anything had actually happened.

Inside the gym, Kaley was waiting by the punch table. Zoey told her about the car, about counting her own pulse. Kaley shrugged. "My sister's in nursing school. She says being nervous makes your body release adrenaline, and it speeds up your heart and pulls blood away from your stomach. That's why it feels like butterflies." Zoey stood very still, working through it. Nothing was wrong with her. Her body was just doing a job, reacting to the idea of the dance instead of the dance itself. If the trigger was the idea, then maybe she could change the idea. She decided to test it.

She found a quiet spot by the trophy case and closed her eyes. She tried to simulate calm, breathing the way she did at the dentist, slow and even, while picturing the gym as just a room with bad lighting and a speaker somebody's cousin had set up. She counted her pulse again. Slower. Not slow, exactly, but slower. Her stomach evened out a little, like a lake after the wind quits. It was working.

Then Elisha crossed the gym toward her, and her heart took off like it had been launched, and she knew, from her own experiment, exactly what that meant. He stopped in front of her and rubbed the back of his neck. "So," he said. "Kaley told me you were counting your heartbeat by the trophies, which is weird, but also kind of interesting."

Zoey laughed, and it came out steadier than she expected. "It dropped twelve beats a minute," she said. "Want to see?" Elisha held out his wrist, and she put her fingers on it, and behind them the first song started pounding through the gym. "Dance first," he said. "Science after."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: For wires of the same material and thickness, doubling the length doubles the resistance.
story:
Laurence spread her notebook on the bench beside the dilapidated climbing frame, where the paint had peeled down to gray metal. The science fair was in four days, and her project, a homemade circuit test, was still missing its best part. She clipped a short piece of nichrome wire between two clamps, touched the battery, and watched the multimeter jump. "Two volts," she announced. "And the current reads one amp."

Carlos leaned over her shoulder, nearly knocking the battery into the wood chips. "So what does that prove?"

"Divide voltage by current and you get resistance," Laurence said, scribbling the number. "Two ohms. That's Ohm's law." She unclipped the wire and held up a longer piece, twice as long, cut from the same spool, the same thickness. "Now the real test."

Yesterday, Mr. Shapiro had handed back her quiz with a note folded inside, and the memory flashed back to her as she worked. "Your reasoning on circuits was excellent," the note read, "but you guessed on the wire question instead of testing it. A scientist does not guess. A scientist measures." She had read it three times on the bus, then dug the multimeter out of her uncle's toolbox that same evening.

She clamped the long wire in place and touched the battery again. Carlos read the screen out loud. "Still two volts. Current is half an amp."

Laurence did the division fast. "Four ohms." Her pencil stopped. "The short wire was two ohms. This one is twice as long and it's twice the resistance." She pulled out a third piece, four times the length of the first, fingers fumbling in her hurry. "If the rule holds, this one has to be eight ohms." Adelie arrived with a juice box just in time to hold the clamps, and they crowded around the meter like it was about to reveal a secret. Two volts. A quarter of an amp. Eight ohms.

"That's the whole project," Laurence said, grinning. "Same material, same thickness, double the length, double the resistance. I can illustrate it with a chart, short wire, long wire, longer wire, bars going up in steps." She started sketching bars right there on the bench. "I'll call the display The Hidden Network Inside a Wire."

Adelie squinted at the spool. "Wait. Did you label these?"

They checked. The short piece and the long piece came from the spool marked nichrome. The third piece, the eight-ohm one, came from a different spool, thinner wire, and had come loose in the same bag. Laurence stared at it, then laughed out loud. Her perfect pattern was built on a stranger's wire. She cut a fresh piece, four lengths of the real spool, and held it out to Carlos.

"Clamp it," she said. "Let's see if the rule survives round two."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: The formula =SUM(B2:B10) adds every cell from B2 to B10; the colon between the two cells marks a range.
story:
Kaylee slid into her seat in the computer lab just as the bell finished ringing. On the screen in front of her was a list of lemonade stand sales, one number for each day of the week, typed in by Mr. Novák for the class assignment. The task was to total the sales and turn them into a bar chart, and Kaylee's problem was bigger than it sounded: her little brother's birthday was Saturday, and she had promised him a bike horn, so she needed to know exactly how much money her stand had earned before she could figure out what she could afford. She had been frugal all summer, saving every quarter, and this spreadsheet held the answer.

She started typing plus signs: =B2+B3+B4. It worked, but by the time she reached B7 her eyes were crossing, and when she checked it against her paper total of the first three days, she had missed a five somewhere. Gia leaned over from the next computer, chewing her pencil. "You're going to be here until the median of forever doing that," she said, nodding at the long chain of plus signs.

A row of gym bags someone had stacked by the door tried to obstruct Kaylee's view of the whiteboard, so she stood up to read it over the pile. Mr. Novák had written one example on the board: =SUM(B2:B10). No plus signs at all. Kaylee sat back down and stared at it. Why two cell names with a colon between them? She had a thought: maybe the colon was like saying "from here to there," a shortcut for everything in between. She typed =SUM(B2:B10) into her total cell and pressed Enter.

The number that appeared was too big. Kaylee frowned, then counted her rows. Her data only went to B8; B9 and B10 were empty. She tried =SUM(B2:B8) and pressed Enter again. This time the total matched her paper, forty-two dollars and fifty cents. "It's a range," she said to Gia, pointing at the colon. "You give it the first cell and the last cell, and it adds everything between." Gia copied the formula into her own sheet and grinned when her total appeared in one step instead of nine.

Zander, two rows back, was still typing plus signs, his shoulders slumped. Kaylee walked over and wrote =SUM(B2:B10) on a sticky note, then changed it to his last row for him and set it beside his keyboard. While he typed it, she went back to her chart, clicked the column of sales, and chose bar chart from the menu. Blue bars climbed across the screen, Saturday's tower rising highest of all. "Forty-two fifty," she told Gia, and started planning which horn to buy.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: When asking a stranger for directions, Spanish speakers usually use the polite usted, French speakers vous, and German speakers Sie, rather than the familiar form.
story:
The phone, which was still under warranty, had died somewhere over the Atlantic, which meant Sophia was navigating Munich with a paper map and a notebook full of phrases she'd copied on the plane. Somewhere between the train station and the museum where her mother was waiting, the streets stopped agreeing with the map. She stood on a corner, feeling defiant about the whole city, and began to formulate her question. She had it almost finished when she caught the little word she'd been about to use, and stopped with her mouth open.

Tatum's texts from Madrid, back when the phone worked, had covered the Spanish part. "Called the shop lady 'tú' and she looked at me like I spilled soup on her cat. It's 'usted' here. USTED." And Winnie, who was in France with her family and wanted nothing more than to win the junior photography contest back home, had sent a postcard of a pastry she clearly cared about more than any museum: "The bakery man liked my picture of his tarts and then corrected me mid-sentence. 'Vous,' he said, right in front of everyone. Anyway the light here would win me that contest, no question."

Sophia also remembered the fall, in Spanish class, when she had asked the teacher where the bathroom was and used the familiar form, and gotten a look she still thought about in quiet moments. Different language, same look, probably. The pattern seemed to be: strangers who were older than you, in Spain and in France, got the polite word. She had no reason to think Germany was the exception, and one reason to think it wasn't: her notebook, copied from the phrasebook, listed "Sie" for exactly this situation. She'd skipped it before because it looked like "she." Now she squared her shoulders.

An older woman with a shopping bag was approaching the corner, walking a small dog that was walking her. "Entschuldigung," Sophia said, and then, carefully, "Wo ist das Museum, bitte? Sie..." She heard the word land and held her breath.

The woman's whole face rearranged itself into something approving. "Sie," she agreed, as if Sophia had passed a small test, and pointed up the street, then left at the tall tower, holding up two fingers for two blocks. Sophia understood every gesture, repeated them back, and got a nod plus one more sentence she caught only half of. "Danke schön," she said anyway.

She found her mother outside the museum doors, ten minutes early. "You made it," her mother said. "With the dead phone?"

"Usted, vous, Sie," Sophia said. "Turns out that's all you really need." Then she turned and waved at the woman with the dog, who was still watching from the corner.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
story:
Ava sat at the kitchen table trying to butter toast with her left hand, which was like watching a seal try to type. The cast ran from her knuckles to her elbow, pale green and already smudged with grape jelly. On the counter sat the walnuts her dad had bought to shell, and next to them the bag of fresh green beans she was supposed to snap for dinner, both jobs she could not do with one working hand.

She kept thinking about what the doctor had said yesterday, mostly because it did not make sense. He had looked at the X-ray, drawn a little arrow with his pen, and told her it was a greenstick fracture, not a regular break. Ava had been too busy staring at the ceiling tiles to ask what that meant, and now the question sat in her head like a pebble in a shoe. Khaled had texted her last night asking if her arm was snapped clean through, and she had answered "sort of," which felt like a lie, since she truly did not know.

The flashback came without being invited. Saturday, the lake, the old wooden dock with its flaking paint. Khadijah had dared her to jump the gap between the dock and the floating swim platform, and Ava remembered standing at the edge, feeling the boards flex under her sneakers. Khadijah had said the jump was easy, and Khaled had said it was a bad idea, and Ava had opposed him out of pure stubbornness, because he was right and she hated that. She remembered the takeoff, the moment her foot slipped, and then the water swallowing her, her forearm cracking against the platform's metal hull as she went under.

Here was what bothered her now, at the kitchen table. The doctor had drawn his arrow on only one side of the bone on the X-ray. One side. If her arm had hit hard enough to break, why would only one side break? She could not see inside her own arm, so she decided to build a model. In the backyard she found a young branch off the lilac bush, still green and bendy, and clamped one end under her shoe.

She pressed down on the other end with her good hand. The branch bent, and bent, and then, with a soft pop, split open on the curved outside while the inside just folded, still connected. She turned it over and looked closely. Cracked on one side, bent on the other. Exactly where the doctor's arrow had been. So that was it, a green branch, a greenstick. Her arm was only partly broken, bent like the branch, and it had happened that way because young bones could bend where old ones would snap. She wondered whether her bones would still do that when she was thirty, and decided she hoped she would never find out.

Khadijah knocked on the back gate that afternoon, holding a bag of gummy worms like a peace offering. "I looked it up," Khadijah said, "because I felt bad about the dare. It's called a greenstick fracture because the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch, and it mostly happens in kids because our bones are more flexible." Ava held up the lilac branch from the table, split side out. "I already did the experiment," she said, and tore the gummy worms open with her teeth.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food banks usually rotate stock by 'first in, first out', sending older items out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves.
story:
The food bank lived in the basement of the public library, in a room that smelled of cardboard and old paper. Louis had agreed to volunteer because his mom signed the form, but now that he was here, he kind of liked it. Rows of shelves stretched under the buzzing lights, and Mr. Rosen handed him a crate of canned beans with a grin.

"New donation," Mr. Rosen said. "Beans go on shelf three."

Louis carried the crate over and found the shelf already half full. He nudged the old cans to the back and stacked the shiny new ones right at the front, where they looked neat and proud, like an emperor's display of treasure. He stepped back, admiring his work, and went to find something else to do.

That was when he heard Mr. Rosen's voice from aisle three, low and puzzled. "That's strange." Louis drifted over. Mr. Rosen was holding a can with a worried frown, and beside him, Winter, another volunteer from school, was peering at the shelf. The can in his hand had a faded label. Expired. Two of them, actually, sitting in the front row.

"Someone put old cans in front of new ones," Mr. Rosen said. "That's backwards. We work first in, first out. Older items go out before newer ones, so less food expires on the shelves. This shelf's been flipped."

Winter groaned. "I did the beans an hour ago. I just stacked the crate where there was room."

Louis's stomach tightened. He had stacked beans too. He watched the shelf like a planet trying to orbit the sun without getting noticed, edging sideways behind a cart of soup. Maybe nobody would check shelf three. His stacking had been quick, and in his hurry, he honestly could not remember which row was which. The lights hummed. Mr. Rosen walked the aisles slowly, running a finger along the cans, and stopped. At shelf three.

"Louis," he called, not unkindly. Louis came, ears hot. "Come look at this." The front of the shelf gleamed with new cans; behind them, crowded and dusty, sat the old ones. Louis's neat emperor row, standing exactly backwards.

"I did that," Louis admitted. "I thought new ones should go in front. I didn't know."

"Then you know now," Mr. Rosen said, and handed him the shelf diagram. "Fix it while I check the pantry."

Louis pulled the new cans off and fed the old ones forward, one by one, until the oldest sat in front like they were first in line. Winter slid in beside him and started on the bottom row. "Faster with two," she said. "Then again, faster still if you'd stacked it right the first time."

"That was almost a compliment," Louis said, and she laughed and tossed him a can of beans.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes when bacteria on the skin break down sweat from armpit glands that become active at puberty.
story:
Zachary sat on the edge of his bed with his gym shirt in his hands, holding it at arm's length like it might bite. He had only worn it for one period of dodgeball, and it had come out of his locker smelling like an old sandwich left in a hot car. In September it had never smelled like anything. He buried his nose in it, gagged, and dropped it on the floor.

His cousin, who was seventeen and visiting for the weekend, had leaned against the doorframe last night and said the strangest thing. "Fresh sweat has almost no smell," he had said. "The stink comes later, when bacteria on your skin break down the sweat from your armpit glands. Those glands don't even turn on until puberty." Zachary had rolled his eyes at the word puberty, but now, alone in his bedroom with the toxic shirt, he turned the idea over. If that was true, then the smell wasn't really his. It was something happening after the fact, like milk going bad on the counter.

He decided to test it. After his shower, he pulled on a clean shirt, did forty jumping jacks in front of his mirror, and worked up a real sweat, the kind that dripped off his chin onto the carpet. Then he lifted his arm and sniffed. Nothing. A little salt, maybe, like the air at the beach, but nothing gross. He wrote it down on a sticky note: 4:02, fresh sweat, no smell.

The dilemma was what to do next. He could wait, but an hour of sitting around seemed like cheating, so he put the same shirt back on after school the next day and let it sit in his locker until Friday. When he sniffed it then, his eyes watered. His note said: 3 days, same shirt, disastrous. He felt weirdly triumphant, like a scientist whose terrible experiment had worked perfectly.

At school he told Dan and Alfred at lunch, because somebody had to know. "The bacteria are the problem, not me," Zachary said. "It's like the shirt is a petri dish and I'm just the delivery guy."

"That is the most disgusting thing you have ever portrayed yourself as," Dan said, but he leaned in anyway.

"So deodorant would fix it?" Alfred asked, looking pessimistic, as if he already suspected the answer was no.

"Deodorant, or washing the shirt before the bacteria finish the job," Zachary said. "New rule for me. Every single day."

That night he stood by his bedroom window with the window cracked open, the cold air washing over him, holding two gym shirts side by side, the clean one smelling like detergent and nothing, the other one still faintly guilty at the corners. He rolled the bad one into a tight ball, carried it down the hall, and dropped it straight into the washing machine.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: USDA guidance says thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) or below.
story:
The lights went out just after sunset, and Annabelle's first thought was the freezer in the pantry room. It was stuffed with the sweet corn and green beans her family had frozen back in August, plus the lamb from Mr. Ramos's flock, and a power cut on a warm September evening was bad news for all of it. She felt along the pantry shelf like a scavenger hunting for the kitchen thermometer, digging past dead flashlights and a bag of rubber bands until her fingers closed around it. The little dial thermometer still worked, and that was something.

She called Bentley first, because Bentley read everything and remembered most of it. "Power's out," she said, holding the phone with her shoulder while she propped the freezer lid open a crack. "I'm trying to figure out how long the food stays good."

"Mom keeps a printout on the fridge," Bentley said. There was a pause, the sound of a drawer being dismantled in the background, screws and junk rattling. "Okay, here. It says thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals, or if it's at forty degrees Fahrenheit or below. That's four degrees Celsius." He read it twice so she could write it down on the back of a seed packet. "So you don't have to chuck everything. Just check it."

Annabelle pressed the thermometer between two bags of corn and waited, counting slowly while her eyes adjusted to the dark. Through the window she could see the whole valley black, no porch lights anywhere, and the arid wind pushing dust across the empty hayfield. Ariel texted from down the road: COME TO THE PORCH, BRING THE MARSHMALLOWS, WE CAN ROAST THEM BEFORE THEY GO BAD. Ariel had been planning a bonfire all week, and a power cut was not going to derail her, apparently.

The thermometer read thirty-eight degrees. Annabelle checked a second bag, then a third, and dug out the lamb, which was still hard as a brick with ice crystals rattling inside the plastic. Everything was below forty or still frosty. She was stacking it all back in when the floor above her shook with footsteps and the lights blazed on, every bulb in the farmhouse at once, and she froze in the glare like a burglar caught mid-crime.

Her mother appeared in the doorway, breathless. "The co-op said a branch took the line, only six houses affected," she said. "How's the food?"

"Safe," Annabelle said, holding up the thermometer. "Thirty-eight degrees. Everything's still got ice crystals anyway, so we can refreeze it all. Bentley's printout says so." She paused, then grinned. "Except the ice cream. The ice cream is soup. I checked that one personally."

Her mother laughed and reached for a spoon. "Then we'd better eat it before it re-refreezes into a brick. Call Ariel. Tell her to bring the marshmallows here."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Placing onion cells in salty water draws water out of them, so the cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall and can be seen; this is called plasmolysis.
story:
The onion field behind Ms. Siddiqui's farm was notorious for two things: mud that swallowed boots whole, and onions so strong that half the class was in tears before the bus even parked. Nobody minded much, because today they were each taking a slice of onion into the barn, where six microscopes waited on a long table next to the hay bales.

Nolan's dilemma was simple. His lab sheet had three boxes to label: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. He could see the wall fine, a tidy row of brick shapes, like a fence around each cell. He found dark dots that had to be nuclei. But the membrane was supposed to be a thin line just inside the wall, and his slide showed nothing. He squinted. He turned the fine focus knob one way, then the other. The line refused to appear.

"Got all three already," said Ekam, who was drawing hers at the next microscope with the calm of someone who had finished a test before anyone else opened their books. Nolan leaned over. Her cells looked the same as his, except hers had a faint inner outline, like a second fence built slightly inside the first. He went back to his slide and felt the small hope he'd been carrying begin to diminish.

Then he thought about it instead of just sulking at it. The membrane was there in every cell, Ms. Siddiqui had said so, and it had to touch the wall, pressed right up against it. Maybe it was invisible because it was too close to the wall to tell apart. He needed the membrane to move, just a little, without breaking anything. What moved a membrane? Water, he guessed. Water moved in and out of cells all the time, so if the water left, the membrane might pull inward, away from the wall, like a curtain drawing back.

He was still working out how to test this when Shawn wandered past holding a salt shaker he'd lifted from the picnic table. "Farm fries later," Shawn said, when Nolan stared at him. Salt. Salt water. Nolan remembered a line from their textbook about salty surroundings and plant cells, and something clicked into place.

"Give me a pinch," Nolan said. He mixed the salt with a drop of water from his bottle, then added one drop to the edge of his slide and watched. Under the lens, the inner outline drew slowly back from the wall in cell after cell, a clean dark gap appearing between the two lines. The membrane had been there the entire time, flattened against the wall where he couldn't pick it apart from it. He labeled all three boxes before his next breath.

Ekam looked over and nodded slowly. "Plasmolysis," she said. "That's what that's called."

Nolan wrote it in the margin, then put his pencil down. "You could have mentioned that twenty minutes ago."

"Where's the fun in that?" said Ekam, and went back to her drawing.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Michael wanted the sneakers more than anything else in the mall. They sat in the window of the shoe store, white with a green stripe, and only fifty pairs had been released in the whole state. To have a chance at buying a pair, you had to post a photo of the store display with the contest hashtag before five o'clock. He had forty minutes.

Denver leaned against the window beside him, tapping his phone. "Travis already posted his. We have to make ours better."

Michael raised his phone and framed the sneakers, but then he paused. Behind the display, reflected in the glass, he could see the whole food court: the pretzel stand, the big blue directory board, and, faint but readable, the name of their mall in curvy letters. Anyone looking at the photo could tell exactly where he was standing. He zoomed in, and the reflection sharpened. There it was, plain as a street sign.

He turned his phone toward Denver. "Look at this. You can see the mall name in the glass."

Denver squinted. "So? Everyone knows the mall."

"Not everyone. Strangers don't." Michael thought about Travis's post. Travis had taken his photo from the other side of the display, near the entrance, and behind him stood the poster with the store's address printed at the bottom in small type. Michael pulled it up and zoomed until the numbers came clear. A stranger who saw it would know the street, the number, and which door to wait at. "Travis is basically telling the whole network where he is."

"That's creepy," Denver said.

Michael negotiated with himself for a second, keeping one prize and giving up another: he would still post, because he wanted the shoes, but he would angle the shot so only the sneakers filled the frame, nothing behind them.
