He stepped closer, crouched, and checked every corner of the picture for reflections, signs, numbers. The food court vanished. Only white leather and a green stripe remained.

He posted it, and they wandered toward the empty end of the mall, where the old fountain had been drained and the hallway felt desolate and cool, smelling of floor polish. His phone buzzed. "Congratulations! You're a finalist," the message said. "Come to the store by five."

They ran past the pretzel stand, sneakers squeaking on the tile, and Michael held the phone up so Denver could read the screen. "Fifty pairs," he panted, "and one of them has my name on it."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
story:
Camille's booth at the cultural festival had to be ready by noon, when the gates opened, and the blank poster board leaning against the folding table was still blank at eleven. She was in charge of the map table, where families would pin cards showing where their ancestors came from. Ryder arrived balancing a box of pushpins, and Kelly carried three markers that smelled like blueberry and lime.

"Look at this," Camille said, holding up a stack of cards people had dropped off early. Every card had a country name in English, except one. A visiting cousin named Fatima had written "Deutschland" in curly letters on the card meant for the Germany pin. Camille frowned at it. Either Fatima had made a mistake, or the whole table was using the wrong names without noticing.

When Fatima came by, Camille asked her about it. Fatima laughed, not meanly, the way you laugh when someone keeps calling your dog by the wrong name. "Deutschland is what we call it," she said. "Germany is what English speakers call it." Kelly tilted her head. "So there are two names for one place?" Mr. Hosseini, checking the loudspeaker at the next booth, shrugged without slowing down. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym," he said over his shoulder, "and a name outsiders use is an exonym." Then he was gone, wrestling with a tangled cord, and Camille was left holding the Deutschland card.

Here was the pattern, she realized, counting the cards: every single one was an exonym, written by someone outside the country naming it. She tested her idea by flipping through the sign-in sheet. Sure enough, families had written their countries in English, even the ones who spoke other languages at home. So the map showed what outsiders called each place, not what the people called themselves. At eleven forty, with the gates opening in twenty minutes, Camille made her decision. She grabbed the lime marker and drew a wide diagonal line across the poster board, splitting it into two halves. LEFT SIDE: THE NAME YOU USE, she wrote. RIGHT SIDE: THE NAME WE USE. "People can contribute both names," she told Ryder. "One card each side. If they only know one, they pin it on that side."

The gates opened at noon exactly. By twelve fifteen, the left half of the map had filled with names Camille had never seen before, and Fatima stood beside her, pinning cards and grinning. But then a woman with a toddler on her hip wrote a name in beautiful looping script on the left side, and Camille realized she had no idea what country it went with, and no pin for it either. "Fatima," she whispered, "we need more pins, and maybe a whole new ocean."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
story:
Nolan arrived at the community art studio on Saturday morning to find Jenny standing at the sink, holding one of the studio brushes up like a strange fossil. It was bent as far as a stick of chalk would bend, which was barely at all.

"Don't bother," she said. "Someone left the whole jar out overnight. Every brush is hard as a stick." She dropped it back into the jar with the others, where they stood up in a clump like tiny trees. Nolan needed those brushes. He was painting a poster for Ms. Van Dijk's mural project, a scene of the river that ran behind the studio, and he had planned to finish the water part today with long, smooth strokes.

He picked up a brush and ran his thumb along the bristles. They were packed together, stiff and shiny. "It's acrylic," he said. "The kind that thins with water when it's wet." Jenny nodded. She had thinned her own acrylics just yesterday, dripping water into a palette cup until the blue ran like juice. "So someone could have washed these out," Nolan said. "They just didn't." He turned the brush under the tap and rubbed the bristles. The warm water slid off them, and nothing softened. He worked at it for a full minute, then set the brush on the paper towel beside the sink, as unbending as before.

"That's bizarre," Jenny said. "If water thins it, why won't water undo it?" Nolan looked at the row of windows where the sun had been baking the shelf all afternoon yesterday, according to Reese, who had been there until closing. He thought about it while he dried his hands. "It dries," he said slowly. "Once it dries, the water doesn't matter anymore. It resists water. That's why you have to wash the brushes before the paint dries on them. Not after." It was the same logic as the sign by the classroom door, but he had never actually seen what happened when somebody ignored it.

"So they're ruined," Jenny said. Nolan wasn't ready to accept that. He filled a jar with hot water and a squirt of dish soap and stood the brushes in it, bristles down, the way he had seen the studio's other painters do. Then he and Jenny walked to the supply desk and asked the cashier, a teenager with paint on her apron, whether the studio had any spare brushes. She found three, thin ones, and a fat flat brush that had a small dent in its handle and was therefore free.

Nolan painted all afternoon. The river came out in long blue and green strokes, and when he made the bank too wide, he let the area dry and revised the shape with a darker green over it, which the wet paint had refused to let him do. Around four o'clock he checked the jar in the sink. Two of the stiff brushes had softened enough to bend. He held one up and flicked it against his palm.

"Look at that," he said, and handed it to Jenny. "Still ugly. But it bends."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Most vegetable seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate, but not light; a few, such as lettuce, sprout better with light and are sown very shallowly.
story:
Sydney pressed her thumb into the soil for the third time that Saturday, checking whether the lettuce seeds she had buried five days ago were still down there. They were. They were also, as far as she could tell, doing absolutely nothing. Beside her, Arham's bean seedlings had already shoved green loops out of the ground, and even Rory's carrots, which Rory watered with the enthusiasm of a puppy and the aim of one, were showing a fringe of feathery leaves.

"Maybe a rodent ate them," Arham offered, crouching beside her plot at the community garden. "A really tiny rodent. With very small hands."

"Seeds don't just vanish," Sydney said, though she wasn't fully sure of that. She was meticulous about recording everything in her notebook: planting depth, watering days, the morning she'd found a soda cap concealing one corner of the soil, which she had removed with great ceremony. Beans, up. Carrots, up. Lettuce, nothing. The pattern bothered her. Same bed, same water, same sun. Why would only the lettuce fail?

She walked over to Ms. Doyle's plot, where the old woman was tying up tomatoes, and asked what depth she used for lettuce. Ms. Doyle held up a pinch of fingers, barely apart. "Barely under," she said. "I just dust soil over them and press lightly, that's all." Then she went back to her tomatoes, humming.

That night Sydney looked it up in the seed packet, then in the library's gardening book, and sat very still for a moment. Most vegetable seeds needed water, oxygen and warmth to germinate, but not light. Lettuce was one of a few that actually sprouted better with light, which was why you sowed it very shallowly. She had dug her seeds down a full inch, deeper than the beans, treating every seed as if it were the same. It wasn't. Ms. Doyle's bare dusting wasn't carelessness; it was the whole point.

On Sunday she raked the bed flat, scattered new seeds across the surface, and sifted the finest dust of soil over them. "You're just throwing them on the ground," Rory said. "That's not planting, that's littering."

"It's planting for lettuce," Sydney said. "They like it shallow. Watch."

By Thursday there were green specks across the bed like spilled pepper. Arham leaned over the border, squinting. "Okay, but if a tiny rodent with small hands shows up, I'm taking credit for the theory."

"You can have the theory," Sydney said, and thumped the watering can down beside his beans. "I'll take the salad."

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: One personal story, called anecdotal evidence, cannot prove a general trend, because a single case may not be typical.
story:
Elliot's palms were sweating onto his note cards, which was bad, because his whole case was written on them. Round two of the regional debate tournament was about to start, and his partner Daniel had exactly one ambition for the day: to say the word "therefore" out loud in a real round, because he'd practiced it in the mirror and thought it sounded impressive. "Focus," Elliot whispered. "Claim, evidence, warrant. We formulated each point that way, remember?"

The topic was whether schools should start an hour later. Elliot and Daniel argued no. Across the table, Diya from Brookside Middle stood up with the confidence of someone who had rehearsed in a bigger mirror than Daniel's. "Schools should start later, because my cousin Maya switched to a late-start school and her grades went way up," she announced. "One person, better grades. That proves the trend."

Elliot blinked. Something felt wrong, like a math problem where the answer came out too tidy. He scribbled on his card: maybe Maya is just good at school anyway? Maybe she'd have gone up no matter what? He couldn't see the whole population of students from here, but he could test the logic the way Ms. Augustin had shown them with a coin: flip it once, get heads, and you've proven nothing about the coin. One case wasn't a window into everyone.

When his turn came, Elliot stood. "Our opponents say one cousin improved, so all students would improve." He held up a single index card with a doodle of a smiley face on it. "This is Larry. Larry likes broccoli. Does that mean everyone at this tournament likes broccoli?" A judge actually snorted. "One personal story is called anecdotal evidence, and it can't prove a general trend, because a single case may not be typical. Diya, is your cousin typical?"

Diya hesitated, then grinned. "She's the least typical person alive. She reads dictionaries at lunch." She turned to her teammate. "I said we needed the study with nine thousand students. You said the cousin story was more memorable." Her teammate, who had been quietly guarding the notecards like a dragon, shrugged. "It was memorable. You're welcome."

The twist came when the judge announced the winner: Brookside, on speaking points. Elliot and Daniel lost the round but won something odd, because the judge added, "Best reasoning in the tournament so far goes to the anecdote rebuttal. That's a separate award." Diya met them in the hallway afterward, holding a trophy she'd won for a case she no longer believed in. "Want to trade?" she said, dangling it. "You give me your rebuttal notes, I'll give you this and my cousin's address, so you can argue with a real dictionary-reader." Daniel reached for the trophy. "Therefore," he said.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies, and the standing water helps keep many weeds from growing.
story:
The departures board flickered to DELAYED just as Jordan set his poster tube down by the seats, and he groaned loudly enough that Ayat looked up from her phone.

"Three hours," she said. "Guess we finally have time for you to practice."

Jordan unrolled the poster he was supposed to present at the science fair in Houston. It showed a map of South Asia with fat red arrows sweeping in from the sea. "Ms. Bakker says I know the facts but can't explain them," he said. "That's like the worst thing to not be able to do."

"Then explain it to me," Ayat said, sliding over to make room. "I'm your test audience. I know nothing."

Jordan took a breath. "Okay. In summer, the land heats up faster than the ocean. Warm air over the land rises, and wet air from the sea rushes in to take its place. That's the monsoon, and it brings months of rain." He pointed at the arrows. "And the rain matters because of rice."

He paused, because this was the part he always fumbled. Ayat leaned forward. "Rice how?"

On the poster was a photo he'd found weeks ago, a green field that looked like a shallow lake, with bright reflections of sky in the water. When he'd first seen it, he'd assumed it was a flood, some kind of disaster. He'd been ready to paste it under a heading about damage until Ms. Bakker asked him one question: "Whose field is that, and who flooded it on purpose?" He'd gone home, looked it up, and sat staring at his screen.

"Those aren't lakes," he said now. "Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies."

"Paddies," Ayat repeated.

"And the standing water helps keep many weeds from growing," Jordan went on, gaining speed. "So when the monsoon comes, farmers aren't hoping the rain stops. They're waiting for it. No monsoon, no water in the paddies, and the weeds move in and the rice fails. Millions of people eat that rice." He tapped the poster. "See? The arrows and the flooded fields are the same story."

Ayat frowned. "But the water sits there for months? Nobody drains it?"

"They don't want to drain it," Jordan said, and then he formulated the idea he'd been circling all week. "The water isn't the problem. The water is the system."

A voice came over the speakers announcing boarding for Houston. Ms. Bakker, three rows back with her carry-on, gave him a thumbs up. Jordan rolled the poster carefully, thinking of his grandfather in the village, who leased his land from the same landlord his father had, and who still watched the sky every June.

"Quiz me again on the plane," he said, tucking the tube under his arm.

"Only if you buy the snacks," said Ayat, and they got in line.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
story:
The scoreboard said eighty-eight degrees, but Liam felt like he was playing inside a wet towel. Sweat ran down his neck and never dried. He remembered a game two weeks ago when it had been ninety-four, and everyone had still felt fine, loose and quick. That made no sense, and it bothered him all through warm-ups on the diamond.

"You look like a peasant hauling rocks," Trace said at the backstop, fanning himself with his cap. "It was hotter at the Ridgefield game and you didn't drag like this."

"That's what I keep thinking," Liam said. He pulled at his soaked sleeve and held his arm in the breeze coming off the outfield. Nothing happened. The air was thick, like the sky itself had been wrung out. He turned to Emmy, who was stretching at first base. "At Ridgefield it was dry. My shirt dried before the second inning. Today it just sits there."

Emmy squinted at him. "So?"

"So maybe that's it. The sweat has to dry to do anything. Today it isn't drying." He thought it through while he took ground balls at shortstop. In dry weather, sweat evaporated fast and that was what cooled you. In this soup of a day, the sweat couldn't go anywhere, so nothing got cooled, and your body just cooked. It would explain why they were all wilting at eighty-eight degrees.

He decided to test it. Between innings he ducked into the dugout and grabbed the water bottle and a paper towel from the first aid kit. In front of Ms. Barrett, who kept the scorebook, he wiped his forearm dry, then waved the towel in the air until it turned faintly damp and cool. "Feel that," he said. "Same air. The towel's drying a little, and it's colder than my arm."

Ms. Barrett touched it and raised an eyebrow. "Evaporation," she said, and went back to her book.

"That's the word," Liam said. He wrote a note in the margin of his hand with a pencil stub, a message for himself to read later: "Next humid day: bench in shade between innings, dry off, cool towels on neck, drink early, because the sweat isn't evaporating and we're not cooling down. Tell Trace." He tucked the paper into his sock and ran back out.

In the fifth inning, he did all of it. He sat in the dugout shade, wiped his face dry, and pressed the damp towel against the back of his neck. By the sixth he was still tired, but he wasn't drowning anymore. He got a clean jump on a ground ball, backhanded it, and threw out the runner by two steps. Trace grinned from the mound. When the half inning ended, Liam jogged to the fence and handed him the towel and the crumpled note from his sock.

"Read it before the seventh," Liam said. "And drink now, not when you're dying."

Trace took a long pull from the water bottle and hung the towel around his neck like a scarf. "Fine," he said. "But if anyone asks, we're not being smart. We're just lucky."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
Bennett sat down at the family computer with a mug of hot chocolate that smelled like burnt marshmallow, because his little brother had "helped" make it. He opened his chat window to find seventeen new messages in the group called Robotics Club But Cooler, and the very first one was a screenshot. He leaned closer to the screen. The screenshot showed a private conversation between him and Lexy from three weeks ago, the one where he'd written that Zoey's robot design looked like a "toaster that a raccoon colonized."

The screenshot had been posted by Zoey herself, with a single message underneath: "cool." Bennett's stomach did a slow flip, like a coin that hadn't decided whether to land on heads or disappear entirely. He scrolled down. Lexy was typing. Then she stopped. Then she was typing again, like she was drafting and deleting an apology the size of a novel.

He remembered exactly how that conversation had happened. It was late, his homework was a chronic disaster, and Lexy had sent him a photo of the robot with a laughing emoji, and he'd typed the raccoon line in about four seconds. He'd thought of it as a private joke between two people. Now it was living in a group chat with eleven people in it, wearing his name like a name tag.

Bennett started typing a defense, then deleted it. Then he typed "that was about the robot not Zoey," and deleted that too, because even he could hear how it sounded. Instead he opened a private message directly to Zoey and wrote, "Can I call you?" His thumb hovered, and the cursor blinked at him, patient and judgmental.

She called instead, voice crackling through his headphones. "So. Raccoons."

"It was about the design," he said. "The wires everywhere. But it came out mean, and I'm sorry." He could hear her chewing gum on the other end, slow and deliberate, like she was deciding whether the apology was artisan quality or mass-produced junk.

"Lexy sent it to me the day you wrote it," Zoey said. "She thought I should know. She wasn't trying to be sneaky about it, she told me afterward. I just sat on it for a while because I was mad, and then today I was mad again, so I posted it." There was a pause with only gum in it. "Honestly, the worst part is that it does look like a raccoon colonized it."

"Eleven people know that now," Bennett said. "I thought private meant private."

"Private means the people in it," Zoey said. "That's it. That's the whole rule." He heard her chair creak as she leaned back. "So next time, maybe don't write anything you wouldn't hand to the person on a poster."

He looked at his half-finished mug, at the little burnt marshmallow still floating in it like a tiny island. "Want me to help rewire the toaster tomorrow? The raccoon and I could apologize in person."

Zoey snorted, and the gum pop that followed was almost as loud as his headphones could handle. "Bring snacks, raccoon boy. Not your brother's marshmallows."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
Zoe's mother managed the Ridgefield Savings Bank, and every Saturday the bank's back room turned into a laundry room where the tellers' white shirts and the new red loan-officer aprons got washed. Zoe had promised to learn the whole job before her mother went on the week-long training course, and today was her first solo run. Brock and Alden had come along because Brock's own mother said he could not leave the house until he learned laundry too, and Alden just liked anywhere with free doughnuts.

"Sort them," Zoe said, pulling shirts from the bin. "Whites here, red aprons there." Brock held up a white shirt and a bright red apron. "They're all clothes. Why does it matter?" Zoe wasn't sure, actually, but her mother's note taped to the machine said to keep them apart, so she did. She loaded the whites, measured the soap, and started the machine while Alden sorted socks into what he called a "coherent system," which was really just two piles.

When the whites came out, Alden pulled a shirt from the drum and went quiet. The collar and sleeves had turned pale pink. Brock leaned in and sniffed it as if smell might solve things. Zoe stood there, thinking. Only the whites had gone pink, and only where they had been wet. She remembered the note on the bin: new aprons, do not mix. New red things, wet white things, pink result. She had an idea, and she wanted to test it before believing it.

She filled the utility sink, a big steel vessel she usually used for soaking, and dropped in one new red apron by itself. While it sat, she made Brock perspire carrying the wet shirts to the dryer, twice, because the cart had a bad wheel. After ten minutes she lifted the apron out. The water in the sink had gone faintly pink, like weak juice, and there were no white shirts anywhere in it. So that was it: the red dye was coming off into the water, and the water carried it into the white fabric. The pink shirts had shared a wash with the new red aprons she had missed, the ones Alden had tucked under the bin lid.

Zoe ran the pink shirts again in plain water, then washed them apart from anything red, and most of the pink faded. She wrote a new note and taped it to the machine. Brock read it aloud: "New dark or bright clothes get their own load. Dye comes off them in the water, and it tints whites and pale stuff." Alden held up the next shirt, checked it against the light, and grinned. "This one's still a little pink," he said. "I'm keeping it. It's a better colour anyway."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The heart naturally speeds up a little on each breath in and slows down a little on each breath out, so slow breathing with long out-breaths helps the heart settle.
story:
The pharmacy smelled like bandages and cherry cough syrup, and Annabelle's heart was going so fast she could feel it in her ears. Her mother had sent her in alone to pick up the refill, but the receipt had gone missing somewhere between the car and the counter, and the line behind her stretched to the birthday cards. Her hands were shaking. She was supposed to give a presentation in Mr. Navarro's class tomorrow, and her body was acting like it was happening right now.

In front of her, a boy about seven years old gripped his mother's sleeve while they waited for his cough medicine. His face was pale. "I hate the doctor part," he whispered, and his mother said they weren't going to the doctor, just the pharmacy. Annabelle watched him breathe. He wasn't gasping. He was counting under his breath, in for three and out for six, over and over, slow and stubborn, like a little generator winding down instead of up. After a minute he looked at his mother and said, "My heart got quiet."

Annabelle could not see her own heart, but she could feel it hammering, and the boy had given her an idea worth testing. She turned the thought over. His out-breaths had been twice as long as his in-breaths, and the calm had come after, not before. Maybe the heart naturally speeds up a little on each breath in and slows down a little on each breath out. If that was the rule, then long, slow breaths out were the lever. She couldn't prove it by looking, but she could run the experiment on herself.

"Next," called the pharmacist. Annabelle stepped up, took a slow breath in through her nose, and let it out for a long count, longer than the in-breath, the way the boy had done. Again. Again. By the third one, the pounding in her ears had softened to something gradual, like rain easing off a roof. She still had to explain the missing receipt, but her voice came out steady. "I don't have the paper," she said, "but my mom's name is on the account." The pharmacist typed, nodded, and slid the white bag across the counter.

Outside, Annabelle texted Kaydence: "Figured out a trick for tomorrow. Meet me before class and I'll show you." Then she sat on the curb and practiced, breathing in for three and out for six, deciding she would do the same tonight before bed instead of lying awake replaying every possible disaster. Tomorrow the presentation would still be scary. But scary with a quiet heart, she thought, was a thing she could work with. She stood, tucked the bag under her arm, and walked back to the car counting softly under her breath.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, which lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure people feel in their ears as a plane descends.
story:
The train hummed along the tracks toward the airport, and Alexia pressed her forehead against the window so she could watch the fields blur together. She was finally on her way to the coast, where her grandmother lived, and she had been counting down the days for a month. Her little brother sat beside their dad, chewing the sleeve of his synthetic rain jacket, which meant he was already nervous about the flight.

"I want window seat," her brother announced, though he had already been promised the window seat three times.

"You'll get it," Alexia said, but she was only half listening. She was thinking about the last time they had flown, two years ago, when he had screamed during the landing so loudly that a man two rows ahead had turned around. It had not been tantrum screaming. It had been hurt. She chewed her pencil, then pulled her notebook out of her backpack and wrote, "landing = pain? why?" Underneath she started a list. "Ears," she wrote, because she remembered him clapping his hands over his ears.

Across the aisle, Mckenzie and Jalen were coming too, on the same school exchange trip, and Mckenzie leaned over now. "What are you writing?" Mckenzie wanted the whole thing to be an adventure, and she had already planned their first afternoon down to the minute.

"Last time we landed, my brother cried like his ears were being squeezed," Alexia said. "And I noticed something. The man next to us was yawning the whole way down, and he looked fine. And the lady across the aisle kept swallowing, like every few seconds. Nobody else looked hurt. Only people who weren't swallowing or yawning." She tapped the notebook. "So maybe the swallowing and yawning were doing something."

"Like a trick?" Jalen said.

"Like opening something in there," Alexia said. "I don't know what. But I have three hours to figure out how to make a four-year-old yawn on purpose."

She tried everything she could think of on the train. She told boring stories to make him yawn. She faked enormous yawns herself, which made him laugh but not copy her. She gave him water to sip, and when he drank it, she wrote "swallowing works, yawning hard" in her notebook. By the time the train reached the airport she was stiff with travel fatigue, and the sun was low, and their boarding was in fifty minutes, which made every line at security feel like a race.

On the plane, the moment the captain announced the descent, Alexia was ready. She had a juice box waiting in the seat pocket, saved from the train station even though the cashier had given her a strange look. "Time for juice," she said, and poked the straw in. Her brother drank, and swallowed, and swallowed again, and his eyes went wide but he did not cry, not once, all the way down.

"Fastest landing ever," Mckenzie announced from the row behind, and Alexia raised the empty juice box like a trophy.

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: Once two triangles are proved congruent, every other pair of matching parts is equal too, a step often written CPCTC: corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent.
story:
The whiteboard in Room 12 smelled like old marker, and Matteo had a plan. Mr. Yamamoto had drawn two triangles, ABC and DEF, and offered a prize: a jar of lemon candies for the first club member who could prove the triangles matched without touching a ruler.

"Side-angle-side," Harrison whispered, leaning over Matteo's desk. "You know that, right? Two sides and the angle squeezed between them."

"I know it," Matteo said, though his confidence had a tendency to evaporate the moment a proof actually began. He copied the triangles into his notebook. AB was marked equal to DE. BC was marked equal to EF. The angle at B, between those two sides, was marked equal to the angle at E. If three of those pieces matched, he thought, the triangles had to be identical, like two keys cut from the same blank.

Ada slid her paper across the aisle. She had already written her proof in purple pen, neat as a row of teeth. "Done," she announced, a little too sweetly.

"Not done," Matteo said, tapping the diagram with his pencil. "Look. The problem asks for AC. The long side across the top. We only know about four sides and two angles."

"So?"

"So we prove the triangles congruent with side-angle-side first. Then the last side comes free." He said it before he fully understood it, and then he did understand it, and it felt like finding a hidden door in a wall. If the whole triangles matched, every matching part matched too. He didn't need to measure AC. It was already trapped, like a fish in a net.

He wrote fast. Given, then statement one, then reason: side-angle-side. Then statement two: AC equals DF. For the reason he hesitated. Across the room, Mr. Yamamoto was pretending to water a plant that was mostly pebbles.

"Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent," Ada said slowly, reading off the poster above the window. "CPCTC. It's right there. It's been right there all year."

"You let me struggle for ten minutes and it's on the wall?"

"The wall is resilient," Ada said. "It can take it."

Matteo laughed so hard he nearly bent his pencil. He wrote CPCTC in block letters, boxed his proof, and walked it to the front. His sneakers squeaked on the tile, and somewhere behind him Harrison was chanting his name like a soccer announcer.

Mr. Yamamoto read the paper twice. He took off his glasses, which was what he did when he was impressed and trying to hide it. Then he opened the lemon candy jar and tipped three candies into Matteo's hand.

"One for you, one for the loud one, one for the one who knew the poster existed."

Ada caught hers out of the air. "Team effort. The estuary of knowledge flows both ways."

"That's not what estuary means," said Harrison.

"Rivers meet the sea, Harrison. Minds meet the math. Keep up."

Matteo popped his candy in his mouth. It was sour enough to make his jaw ache, and he grinned through it, already flipping to the next problem.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
story:
Victoria had one job at Casey's house: finish the science fair project about memory. Casey's older sister had left a psychology textbook open on the kitchen table, and one paragraph stopped Victoria cold. It described a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, where people who were asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people who were asked how fast cars hit.

"Read this," Victoria said, pushing the book across the table. Casey read it, shrugged, and went back to eating cereal at eleven in the morning, lethargic in a way that only Saturdays allowed.

"It's saying the question changes the answer," Victoria said. "The word changes the memory." Casey pointed his spoon at her. "Then prove it. My parents totally fell for stuff like that. Plus I need entertainment."

The opportunity arrived sooner than expected. Casey's little brother came inside crying, holding his elbow. He announced that he had crashed his scooter into the recycling bin. Victoria knelt down, kept her voice flat, and asked, "How fast were you going when you smashed into that bin?"

"Super fast," he sniffled. "Like really really fast." He held his hands apart the width of a small car. Then Casey asked the same brother the same question on the walk to the park, using the word hit, and the boy estimated a speed so slow Victoria scrutinized his face to check whether he was joking. He was not. Same scooter, same bin, same elbow, two different memories of the speed.

They spent the afternoon designing a real test. They filmed two friends on Casey's street who agreed to watch a video of two shopping carts rolling into each other, then answer one question. The smash group said the carts were flying. The hit group said they barely moved. Victoria kept a tally in her notebook and drew a bar graph with a ruler borrowed from Casey's dad, who wandered through and said the whole economy of the household would collapse if anyone else touched his ruler.

At dinner, Casey's mother asked what they had been doing all day. Casey started to explain, got tangled, and gestured at Victoria with a fork. Victoria laid out the study, the scooter experiment, and the shopping cart graph, in that order. Casey's mother looked at her own son. "Wait. Is this why my questions keep coming out sounding like evidence in a courtroom?"

"Probably," Casey said. "It's science now. We're immune."

"You're not immune," said his little brother. "You cried when the coach asked if you got clobbered at practice."

"Let it go," Casey said.

"I got clobbered. She asked. I remembered it."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
story:
Elijah sat cross-legged on Charlie's bedroom floor with the phone box open in front of him like a treasure chest. The phone itself was nothing fancy, a hand-me-down from his cousin with a small crack in the corner, but it was his first one ever. Charlie leaned over his shoulder while Sofie spun slowly in the desk chair, waiting to help. "First thing you do is set up your account," Charlie said. "Then we can text each other dumb stuff at midnight." "My mom says she supervises my phone for the first month," Elijah said. "She checks the screen time report every Sunday." Sofie grinned. "Mine too. It's annoying but honestly I'd probably never sleep."

Setting up the account took forever. He had to choose a password, and Charlie made him use a real one, not "password123," because Charlie's older brother had done that once and lived to regret it. Elijah typed in something long with numbers and a symbol, then had to type it again to confirm it. Then came the email, then the app store, and by the time all of it was done, the afternoon had gone barren and gray outside the window, the trees stripped and the sky the color of wet chalk. Sofie suggested they play a board game to give their eyes a break.

They were halfway through a round of checkers when Elijah's new phone buzzed on the rug. He picked it up and frowned. "That's weird," he said. "It says my login code is 4-8-2-9-1. It's asking if that's me." He showed them the message. "But I'm not logging into anything. I'm sitting right here." Charlie scratched his head. "Maybe it's a glitch. My dad's phone does random stuff all the time." But Sofie sat forward in the chair. "Or maybe it's not a glitch. My mom got one of those once, and it turned out somebody else was typing her password from their own computer, trying to get in. The code went to her phone, not theirs, so they couldn't finish."

Elijah turned the phone over in his hands, thinking. If someone was logging in as him, that meant one thing: someone had his password. He had only known the password for three hours. He tested the idea in his head like a math problem. The code text arrives only when someone enters the password correctly. He hadn't entered anything. Therefore someone else had. "Wait," he said slowly. "I told my cousin my new password this morning over text, on my mom's phone. His account might still be logged in on the old phone before he wiped it, or he told somebody." It didn't matter exactly who; what mattered was that the password was already loose in the world.

"So what do you do?" Charlie asked. Elijah remembered the setup screen from earlier, something he had skipped past because it seemed boring. He picked up the phone and dug back into the settings until he found it. "This," he said, and tapped to turn it on. "My cousin called it two-factor authentication. It means you need a second proof, like a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in." Sofie nodded. "That's why my mom's hacker failed. They had the password but not her phone." Elijah changed his password too, to one he told absolutely nobody, not even out loud to the empty room.

Then he had another thought, and this one he tested right away. He handed the phone to Charlie. "Try to log into my account from your tablet. Use the old password, the one that might be stolen." Charlie pulled up the login page and typed it in. A moment later, Elijah's phone buzzed with a new code request, and Charlie's tablet showed a box asking for a code that only Elijah could see. "I can't get any further," Charlie said, poking at the screen. "It just wants that code." Elijah felt something loosen in his chest, like a knot untying. "Exactly. That's the whole point."

Ms. García, Charlie's neighbor, knocked on the door frame to return a borrowed board game and found the three of them celebrating over a cracked phone. "Something good happen?" she asked. "My account got attacked and I stopped it," Elijah said. "Sort of by accident, but still." She laughed and said that was more than most adults could claim. After she left, Sofie set up the last piece of the evening: a group chat with the three of them, named "Midnight Dumb Stuff." Elijah's first message was a single thumbs-up. Charlie replied in two seconds flat.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
The group chat was called Worm Team Six, because their science project was about earthworms, and Dexter refused to let anyone forget it. He was diligent about the research, always the first to post facts, and that afternoon he sent a wall of messages. "Earthworms decompose dead leaves and turn them into soil," he typed. "Also a robin is technically not an herbivore because it eats worms, which I think is rude of the robin." Rosalie laughed, but she noticed Celina hadn't replied in two days, which was strange, because Celina usually sent the most messages of anyone.

Rosalie looked back through the chat, scrolling slowly, hunting for a pattern. Celina had gone quiet right after Dexter posted screenshots of the chat in the class forum so everyone could see the funny robin joke. Before that, Celina had seemed fine. Before that, Dexter had read Celina's rough draft aloud in class without asking, and Celina had gone quiet then too. Rosalie chewed her pencil. Something invisible was going on, and she had a guess about it, but a guess wasn't proof. She decided to test it the way Ms. Abdi had shown them for the worm experiment: change one thing, watch what happens.

First she messaged Dexter directly. "Can you not post screenshots of our chat without asking?" she typed. He replied with a single confused emoji, then, "ok?" Rosalie waited. Within an hour, Celina was back in the chat, posting a drawing of a worm in a tiny party hat. That was the evidence. Rosalie messaged her privately. "You went quiet when Dexter shared our stuff. Was that it?"

Celina took a long time to answer, long enough for Rosalie to feel her own stress rising. Then: "Yeah. I should have said something instead of just disappearing. My counselor calls it a boundary. It's a limit you set about what you're comfortable with, like how people treat you or use your stuff." Rosalie read it twice. "I think I set one today," she typed. "I told Dexter to ask before he screenshots." Celina sent back a row of exclamation points.

The next morning Ms. Abdi collected their project outline and told the Worm Team their careful notes were the best in the class. But Rosalie was prouder of something smaller. When Dexter wanted to share their worm video with his cousin, he actually asked first, in the chat, in front of everyone. "Is that ok with you guys? Celina, Rosalie, anybody objecting?"

"Objection withdrawn," Celina typed. "Post it."

Rosalie smiled at her screen and typed, "Approved. Robin discretion still advised."
